earlier_scan.source_named: Read Cahill 1992, A Preliminary Phonology of the Konni Language (archive.org rosettaproject_kma_phon-1 fulltext): tonal analysis throughout, zero stress/prominence statement found

new_statements.quote: In this phonology, I have not mentioned stress as a relevant quality of words. Most Gur phonological write-ups also do not discuss stress. [...] In Konni, there do not seem to be any phonetic correlates of stress (vowel length, amplitude) which are significant and independent of tone. [...] Note above that while the first two syllables in both words (spoken in isolation in the same recording session) are LH, in (A) the second syllable has greater amplitude, while in (B) the first syllable has greater amplitude. If "articulatory energy" is what the other Gur writers are referring to when they speak of "stress", then this does not seem to be consistent in Konni. Though more research undoubtedly needs to be done in this area, it appears that stress is not phonologically contrastive or distinctive in Konni. (pp. 465-466) — p. 39: 'Since some African languages have been analyzed as having stress, the question is examined for Konni, with the conclusion that stress plays no part in the phonology of Konni.'

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has no record for konn1242 and no existing statements; this is the first explicit stress statement found for the language. The open_url was the the Harvard library catalogue discovery record, which points to OhioLINK ETD osu1488190595942418; the PDF was downloaded directly from the OhioLINK ETD send_file endpoint (open access, 17.1 MB, ABBYY text layer, 560 PDF pages).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kɔnni has two basic tone levels, High and Low, plus a downstepped High (p. 338). Cahill looks for stress explicitly and finds no phonetic correlate (vowel length, amplitude) that is significant and independent of tone; amplitude peaks fall on different syllables in the two measured words (kùlî 'tortoise' vs kùléhé 'the tortoises'); his conclusion is that stress is not phonologically contrastive or distinctive and plays no part in the phonology. No stress position is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Author hedges: 'more research undoubtedly needs to be done in this area'. He notes that other Gur descriptions (Dagaare: Antilla & Bodomo 1996; Supyire: Carlson 1994; Buli: Kroger 1992) speak of stress on penultimate or root-initial syllables or of greater 'articulatory energy' on initial syllables, and suggests word-initial position rather than stress may be the relevant property there.
new_statements.identity_note: Cahill 1999 describes Kɔnni of Yikpabongo, Northern Region, Ghana (the only variety in the literature); no dialect split is at issue. Works 4 and 5 (Berwick & Chomsky 2019; Rezac 2004) are not about Kɔnni at all and appear to be Glottolog misattributions; works 6 and 7 are cross-linguistic SIL working papers.
